_: Source of truth for the lesson videos. One video per lesson in src/data/lessons.ts, in that order. Each video is the lesson page filmed (series/PAGE-BUILD.md): lines here are the narration, lessons/<id>/page.json says what is on screen for each. tools/series.mjs renders series/index.html for review and --emit writes lessons/<id>/script.json.

videos.title: Workshop Overview
videos.opensFrom: The start of the course: nothing read, nothing installed, nothing on the bench yet.
videos.handsTo: Prerequisites is every download and account, finished before any hardware gets plugged in.
lines: This is the start of the course, so there's nothing to look back on yet. What's ahead runs from one small mechanism on a bench all the way to a swerve drive.
You don't need to have written code before. What you do need is a mechanism, because the whole course is built around running one.
People trip on the phrase hardware simulation. It sounds like nothing real is involved, but the only part being stood in for is the robot controller, and your laptop plays that role.
Everything else is real. The motors spin, the bus carries real messages, and the arm on your bench is the one that moves.
The code is written for CTRE devices and nothing else. With other motor controllers the ideas still carry over, but the examples won't run as written.
For 2027 the way you write robot code changed, and this course teaches the new style from the start. Plan on a SystemCore when you move to a robot, because a roboRIO can't run it.
Both libraries are alpha releases, which means things can shift between builds. Project Setup pins the exact versions, so match them when you get there.
The language card is a quick test for any example you find online. If its package names don't start the way these do, it was written for an older year.
Go in order. Each workshop leans on the hardware or the code from the one before it.
Nothing runs on this page, so the check is short and honest. The mechanism has to be in front of you and powered, not still on a purchase order.
The laptop matters just as much. The next page is all downloads and accounts, and you'll want every one finished before anything gets plugged in.

videos.title: Prerequisites
videos.opensFrom: Workshop Overview laid out what the course teaches and the hardware and 2027 stack it runs on; nothing is installed yet.
videos.handsTo: Hardware Setup plugs the CANivore in and finds every device in Tuner X; Mechanism CAD sits in between for teams that still have to build.
lines: The overview laid out where this course is headed. Before it can start there are two lists to finish, and most of that time goes to watching installers run.
Five programs, in any order you like. Notice what's missing, though. You don't install Java yourself, because the first program brings the right version with it.
The first one is where people go wrong. The official install guide still sends you to last season, so use the link here and take the alpha by its exact version.
A newer alpha is already out, and grabbing the latest feels safe. Don't. The course is staying on this one for now.
Tuner X is the program you'll open first and use the most. All of Workshop 1 happens inside it, before you've written any code at all.
Alpha means the tools are still moving. Something in an example here could be renamed before the season starts, so don't be surprised when one changes.
Never written Java? That's fine. It gets taught in Workshop 2, and the code is explained as it shows up.
Now the bench. For all of Workshop 1 your laptop runs the mechanism directly, and that's why the hardware list is so short.
The CANivore is what joins the two halves. It plugs into a USB port on your laptop, and the name you give it now gets used again in Workshop 3.
Bench tests only use a volt or two, but that's no reason to skip the battery. The motor still needs a real, charged one behind it.
Here's what you don't need: a robot. One mechanism on a table with a laptop beside it is the whole rig.
Before you leave, open each program once. You're only checking that it starts without an error, so empty windows and red lights are exactly right for now.
Once all three are true, the waiting is over. Next you plug the CANivore in and find out whether Tuner X can see every device on it.

videos.title: Mechanism CAD
videos.opensFrom: Prerequisites put the software half on the laptop and said the hardware half sits on the bench.
videos.handsTo: Hardware Setup takes the assembled, wired mechanism and powers it up for the first time, with nothing turning yet.
videos.gate: A scripted demo of the page's interactive.
lines: The prerequisites put the software on your laptop. The other half is a mechanism on the bench, and this is where it comes from. If you've already got one, skip ahead.
It's really one build with two endings. The frame and the gearbox are the same either way, so most of what you buy for one goes straight into the other.
Here's the flywheel. A wheel on each end of the shaft and no extra sensor, because the motor already has one inside it.
And the arm. The part to find sits right at the joint, an encoder that reads the angle of the tube.
Turn it around before you build it. The buttons under each model snap to a fixed view, so you can see how the pieces stack up.
There are three ways to take a model with you. If you only want to print a part, grab the first. If something has to change size, you'll need the second.
All new, the price looks like a lot, and most of it is CTRE hardware. Tick the boxes for parts you already own and parts you can print, and the arm drops to a fraction of that.
The most expensive row on either list is the CANivore, and one of them runs both builds. Check the shelf before it goes on the order.
You can even print the gearbox. The bought kit comes with its bearings and long screws and a printed one doesn't, so those stay on your list.
Two of the build notes matter more than the rest. Every T-nut goes into the extrusion before the end cap does, because adding one later means pulling the cap back off.
And the battery never clips straight onto the mechanism. The clips come off the adapter cable, and its leads go into the lever nuts.
Before any of it sees power, turn it by hand. If the arm goes all the way around and nothing rubs the encoder, it's ready to be powered up. That's next.

videos.title: Hardware Setup
videos.opensFrom: Prerequisites installed Phoenix Tuner X, and Mechanism CAD left an assembled, wired mechanism with a charged battery.
videos.handsTo: Every device is on the bus with current firmware; Motor Setup gives each one its own CAN ID and makes the first motion.
lines: Your mechanism is built and wired, and Tuner X is already on your laptop. Today they meet. Get this part wrong, and every later lesson is spent fighting the hardware.
Start with the motor. Its controller is built into the back, and it reports its own position so you already have one sensor before you add anything.
So why does the arm get a second one? The motor's own count starts from zero wherever it sits at boot. This encoder reads a magnet on the shaft, and it remembers the angle with the power off.
The CANivore is the reason you don't need a robot yet. Your laptop plugs into it over USB, and it carries the conversation to everything else.
If you built the flywheel, skip the encoder everywhere it comes up. A flywheel only cares about speed, and the motor measures that by itself.
Order matters here. Power goes on first, then the USB cable. After that, Tuner X needs two settings changed, and neither one is a team number.
Step four is the one that bites later. The name you type has to match the code in every lesson that follows, so spell it exactly as it's shown.
A device in the list isn't proof of anything, because old firmware connects and answers just the same. Update the CANivore first, then everything else.
Once the flashing finishes, the card colours do the checking for you. Green is what you want on every card. Yellow means there's still an update waiting.
Red isn't a firmware problem at all. Two devices are answering to the same number, and that's the next lesson's job.
Now pull the battery and the USB, and bring both back. Nothing should be lost, since the name and the firmware live on the devices themselves.
On an arm there's one more test. Turn it by hand and watch the encoder's position change on screen. Everything's on the bus and current, so next, each device gets its own number.

videos.title: Motor Setup & CAN IDs
videos.opensFrom: The mechanism is powered, the firmware is current and Tuner X sees every device; nothing has turned yet.
videos.handsTo: Voltage Out pushed a volt with no target and no place to stop; PID Tuning gives the motor a target.
lines: Your bench is powered and showing up in Tuner X, and nothing has turned yet. Before anything does, each device needs its own number and the right settings.
These are the numbers the rest of this page uses. Set the rows for the hardware you've got.
A factory default wipes nearly everything, but it leaves the ID alone. So if two devices flash on one blink, they're sharing a number, and one has to move first.
Blink is how you know which device you're about to change. A name in a list proves nothing until a light on the bench flashes back.
None of it is saved until you press Apply. It's a small arrow, and it writes settings to the device, not firmware.
On the arm, direction comes first, and you check it by hand. The motor's position should climb as you turn the arm counterclockwise, with the motor facing you.
The encoder gets the same hand test. Then you pick the spot that counts as zero, and a quarter turn from there should read about a quarter of a rotation.
Rotations, not degrees. Counterclockwise is positive, and every position target from here on is written that way.
Only now do you link the two. Link them while they count in opposite directions and every lesson after this one breaks, so finish with one more turn by hand.
Now the first motion under power. Voltage Out sends a fixed voltage with no target, and it won't stop at the end of travel. You stop it.
So start at one volt and enable for about a second. Blink first, too, because the voltage goes to an ID, not to the device you had in mind.
If the arm turns clockwise, don't fix it here. It means a hand test was skipped or never applied, so go back and redo them.
Power the bench down, bring it back, and walk these checks. Once positive means the same direction by hand and under power, the motor is ready for a target. That's PID tuning.

videos.title: PID Tuning in Tuner X
videos.opensFrom: Voltage Out pushed one volt with no target and no place to stop; now the motor gets a target.
videos.handsTo: The target here jumps all at once; Motion Magic walks it there instead, on the same gains.
videos.gate: A scripted demo of the page's interactive.
lines: Last time you sent the motor one volt, and it had no idea where to stop. Now it gets a target, and the motor itself does the work of getting there.
CTRE's own tuning guide is the one to follow. The steps here are the same method rewritten in volts, for when you can't reach it.
Before you touch the real mechanism, break this one. Every gain starts at zero, and a bad number costs you nothing.
Try it. Push the proportional gain up until the arm swings past its target, and watch the trace.
Every gain on this page is volts for each rotation. A number copied from a guide that uses different units won't mean the same thing here.
The plot is how you'll judge every change, so set it up first. Both signals go in one group, and the timespan comes way down, because it's counted in minutes.
A gain you type does nothing until you press Apply. If a change seems to have no effect, check that before you change it again.
Start with every gain at zero. Whatever the mechanism does after that, you'll know which number caused it.
Feedforward comes first. Find the smallest and the largest gravity gain that hold the arm level, and what you want sits in the middle.
Then feedback. Keep doubling the proportional gain until it overshoots, back off to about half, and let a little derivative take out the rest.
When it goes wrong, read the plot. Error that keeps growing means a direction is backwards, so disable right away. A hum at rest is too much gain, and more damping won't fix it.
You're done when three runs each way look alike. The target still jumps there all at once, though, and smoothing that out is the next lesson.

videos.title: Motion Magic in Tuner X
videos.opensFrom: PID Tuning left trusted Slot 0 gains and a plot of target against measurement, with a target that still jumps to the end all at once.
videos.handsTo: Everything so far was done by clicking in Tuner X; Java Basics starts on the language that will ask for the same moves in code.
lines: Your gains are saved, and three runs each way look alike. The target still jumps to the end in one step, though, so the loop gets asked for the whole move at once.
None of that tuning gets thrown away. Motion Magic only changes the target your gains are chasing, so keep the same plot open and leave Slot 0 alone.
Two limits shape the trip. One is a top speed, and the other is how quickly the mechanism may build up to it. Jerk you can ignore unless your mechanism is very heavy.
An arm is going somewhere, so its plan includes the stop. A flywheel never arrives anywhere, which is why it only gets a ramp.
Start much slower than you think you need, because the first run is only there to show you what the profile does. Check the units too. They count turns of the mechanism, not the motor.
Nothing changes until you switch the control mode over on the Control tab. The limits themselves go in the Motion Magic section of the configs.
Switching the mode also disabled the motor. If you press Apply and nothing moves, that's the reason, so enable it again before you run anything.
Once it follows the profile cleanly on every run, raise the limits a step at a time. You stop when the measurement falls behind, the current spikes, or the structure shakes.
Then try the longest move you'll ever ask for, both ways, and the shortest. A short one never gets up to cruising speed, so what it really tests is the stop.
Don't keep the best numbers you found. A battery late in a match can't keep up with what it managed fresh, so back the limits off and leave some room.
Five runs with the traces stacked on each other, and the motor plans its own way there. All of it happened by clicking. Next you start on Java, so code can ask for the same move.

videos.title: Java Basics
videos.opensFrom: Workshop 1 tuned the mechanism in Tuner X without a line of code; the code starts here.
videos.handsTo: A command gets built here and nothing runs it; The Command Framework introduces the scheduler that does.
lines: Everything you've done so far happened in Tuner X, with no code at all. From here on you write it, and this page is the short list of Java you'll want first.
If Java is new to you, start with this free course. Four modules is plenty, and the third one is what the robot code leans on hardest.
Then stop. There's more Java after that, but nothing in this workshop uses it, and we'll fill in the rest as it comes up.
These six words show up in every lesson after this one. The course teaches five of them.
The constructor runs once, at the moment the arm is built. That makes it the place for anything that should only happen a single time, like setting up a motor.
The lambda is the odd one out. That little arrow turns the code after it into a parcel, written down and handed over instead of run.
You'll also call methods you can't find anywhere in your own file. One word on the class line is why, because the arm gets everything a mechanism can do without writing any of it.
Here's all of that in one real method from the arm. A name and a return type on top, then a lambda in the middle with dots chaining the calls around it.
This is the part people miss. Calling that method doesn't move the arm. You get a command back with the parcel inside, and it sits there until something else runs it.
Five questions tell you whether this stuck, so miss more than one and go back to the course. After that, you'll meet the thing that actually runs the command.

videos.title: The Command Framework
videos.opensFrom: Java Basics ended on a method that builds a command and hands it back with the lambda parked inside, for something else to run later.
videos.handsTo: Project Setup generates the robot project that the scheduler call, the mechanisms and the mode classes all go into.
lines: Last time, a command came back with its code parked inside, waiting for something else to run it. Here's that something else.
Each part answers a question. A trigger is when and a mechanism is what moves, with a command in between saying how. The coroutine is just the steps inside that command.
None of them runs by itself. Fifty times a second the robot calls this one method, and the single line inside it gives the scheduler its turn.
Each turn it checks every trigger, then starts and cancels commands from what it found. Delete that line and nothing on the robot ever runs.
A command built inside a mechanism owns it while it runs, which keeps two commands from driving one motor at once.
So what happens when a second command wants the arm? Every command here has the same priority, so the newcomer takes it and the old one is canceled.
Canceled doesn't mean stopped. When nothing owns the arm, nothing is talking to its motor, and it carries on with the last request it was given.
Mechanisms and the driver's controller get created once, in the same file as the scheduler call, and they're public so every mode can reach them.
What the robot does with them is up to a mode. Each is its own class, and the marking on top puts it in the driver station's list.
Button bindings go in the mode's constructor. The class is built when someone picks the mode and thrown away on a switch, so a binding from auto can't fire in teleop.
Most commands in this course run their body every loop and never finish, so something outside has to end them.
Here a trigger does it. Letting go cancels the running command, and the second half of the line starts the one that stops the motor.
Before you move on, work out who owns the arm before the press, during the hold and after the release. Next you'll make the project all this code goes into.

videos.title: Project Setup
videos.opensFrom: The Command Framework named the four parts of robot code, triggers, coroutines, commands and mechanisms, with no project yet to put them in.
videos.handsTo: Mechanisms writes the first class, an arm or a flywheel, inside the project that builds clean here.
lines: You know the parts of robot code now: triggers, commands, mechanisms. None of them has anywhere to live yet, so you make the project yourself.
It all starts from one small red icon in the title bar. If you can't find it, you've opened the ordinary editor, not the one the installer gave you.
Pick the template. An example is a finished robot that somebody else wrote, and you're here to write your own.
The second page has a long list, and a couple of entries sound right. Only one matches the code you'll be typing for the rest of the course.
Slow down on the third page. Two of these four fields cause real trouble later if you get them wrong.
The checkbox is the easy one to miss. Without it the program can't run on your laptop, and running it on the laptop is how Workshop 3 drives the real motors.
Then the folder path. Cloud sync rewrites files while the build is using them, and the failure looks like a mistake in your code. School laptops often sync Documents and Desktop without telling you.
The skeleton switches on a second logging tool this course doesn't use. Take those four lines out, or every mechanism gets logged twice and each build prints a note for every field it can't log.
It also ships with nothing for the driver station to pick. You make the teleop file by hand, and keep its name exactly as written, because every lesson after this one opens it.

The command library came with the template. The motor controllers' library didn't. Watch which one you install, because a library with nearly the same name sits right underneath it, and it's the wrong one.
Changing a library kicks off a build by itself. Leave it alone. The first one has a lot to download, so it's slow, and later ones won't be.
If it stops because it couldn't resolve something, that's the network, not you. Reconnect, then run the build again from the same red icon.
You're done when the build ends in success and your file tree matches this list. That's an empty robot that builds, and the next lesson puts the first mechanism in it.

videos.title: Mechanisms
videos.opensFrom: Project Setup ended on an empty robot project that builds clean, with no mechanism in it.
videos.handsTo: Writing Commands turns the two private methods written here into commands a button can run.
lines: Your project builds, and there's nothing in it yet. The first class you write by hand is one physical part of the robot. We'll follow the arm.
Where the file lands matters. The new folder has to sit right beside the robot class, and one made a level up puts your code in the wrong package.
You start from a template, and most of its imports will be greyed out. That's fine. They wake up as you fill the class in.
The fields are the hardware you already met in Tuner X: the bus, the motor, and the CANcoder. If your bench came out with different numbers, change the code to match.
Watch the bus name. It has to be spelled the way you named it in Tuner X, or nothing answers.
You don't type the configuration. Tuner X already has it, so it writes the code and you paste that into the constructor.
The config printed on the page is ours, there for its shape. Paste your own over the whole thing, and if your gains come along, leave them in.
For the arm, one part of that config matters most. The motor's own count starts from zero at every power-on, so the config points it at the absolute encoder instead.
Two short methods finish the class. One sets the number on the request you built as a field and sends it. The other stops the motor, and Coast takes over.
Plain voltage is only a simple test. This table is the rest of the family, and the one you finished Workshop 1 on drops in just as easily.
A motor keeps applying the last request it got, even after the code that sent it has stopped running. That's what the stop method is for.
The robot class gets one field for the arm. It's public, so every OpMode you write later can reach it.
Nothing here moves a motor, so the check is a clean build. Both methods are still private and nothing calls them, and turning them into commands is the next lesson.

videos.title: Writing Commands
videos.opensFrom: Mechanisms left the arm and the flywheel each with a motor and two private methods that nothing outside the class can call.
videos.handsTo: Three commands exist on each mechanism and nothing runs them yet; OpModes puts them on the controller's buttons.
lines: Last lesson left the arm with a working motor and two private methods, and nothing outside that class can reach them. A command is how the rest of the robot gets to ask.
It's also what keeps things safe. The scheduler gives the arm to one command at a time, so two pieces of code can't both be driving the same motor.
One import comes first. Watch the package name as it goes in, because getting it wrong is one of the two build errors waiting at the bottom of this page.
Here's the first command. The method is public, so anything can ask for it, while the setter it wraps stays private.
The other two are built the same way. One pushes harder, and one stops the motor.
That arrow is the lambda from Java Basics. It doesn't push the motor right there. It packs the call up and hands it over, to be made once every loop.
The name on the end isn't decoration. Until it's attached, what you have is only half built, and the build won't accept it.
None of the three has an exit. Each keeps running until something else claims the arm, and even the stop sends its zero every loop, because canceling a command doesn't stop a motor.
So nothing should ever wait for one of these to end. It'd wait forever. A routine asks a question about the mechanism instead, and writing that question comes later.
Now build. If it fails, check these two before anything else: a command that's missing its name, or the import that never went in.
That's three commands on the arm, and so far nothing runs any of them. The controller's buttons do that, and wiring those up is the next lesson.

videos.title: OpModes
videos.opensFrom: Writing Commands left three commands on the mechanism, building clean, with nothing yet that runs them.
videos.handsTo: Hardware Simulation runs these bindings for the first time and shows why every one of them needs a release.
lines: You've got three commands on your mechanism, and nothing that runs them yet. This is where one of them gets a button.
You made this teleop file yourself in Project Setup. The annotation on the class is what puts it on the driver station, and without it there's nothing to choose.
So far it's one empty constructor, and this lesson fills it. Edit this file and don't make a new one, because a second teleop class means two teleops on the list.
The controller goes in the robot class, right beside the mechanisms. Put it there once, and every OpMode you ever write reaches it the same way.
It's two additions. The import goes up top, then the field, and the zero is the port the controller sits on at the driver station.
Now the teleop itself. Its whole contents get replaced, and what's left is short: one class, one constructor, one binding.
The constructor is handed the robot. That's how this file gets to your mechanism, and to the controller you just added.
Read the binding left to right. It picks the left trigger, and the first half runs the fast command for as long as the trigger's held, then cancels it when you let go.
The second half covers the release. Once the trigger comes up it runs a command of its own, and here that's stop.
A passing build isn't enough here, because nothing moves yet. Search the folder for the teleop annotation too, and make sure it turns up exactly once.
Every binding line gets a release. Why it needs one is something you'll see for yourself next, in Hardware Simulation, when you finally pull the trigger.

videos.title: Hardware Simulation
videos.opensFrom: OpModes bound the controller's buttons to the commands in MyTeleop, each hold with a release, and nothing has run on the bench yet.
videos.handsTo: Motion Magic in Code sends a position request instead of a voltage, where a request that stays on the motor after the release is what holds the arm in place.
videos.gate: A scripted demo of the page's interactive.
lines: Your buttons are bound, but none of that code has turned a motor yet. Now the laptop plays the robot controller, and everything past it is real.
Tuner X and your program can't both have the devices. Turn that switch back off, or no motor ever answers your code.
These are real motors. Clear the arm's path, and know where Disable is.
Two entries sit right next to each other in this menu. Pick the one with Hardware in its name. The other fakes the motors, and your bench won't move.
Drag your controller onto the first slot. That's the port your code listens on.
Pick Teleoperated, then your OpMode under it. Your real devices show up on the right, and an empty list means you started the wrong simulator.
Enable, and nothing moves, which is correct. Every command is waiting on a button. Hold one and the mechanism runs, then let go and the release binding takes over.
So what about a binding with no release? This diagram follows one press from the controller, through your code, out to the motor controller.
Hold the button, and the command sends six volts every loop while the motor runs. Now let go.
The command is gone and the motor's still turning. Canceling a command sends the motor nothing, so it carries on with its last request.
Tick the box, and the release gets a command of its own, one that sends the motor something new.
Try it again. Hold the button, let go, and watch what reaches the motor this time.
A request stays on the motor until another one replaces it. For every button you bind, decide what the release sends.
A real robot gets this same program from the same menu. Next the arm gets a target instead of a voltage, and there a request that stays put is exactly what you want.

videos.title: Motion Magic in Code
videos.opensFrom: Hardware Simulation ran the voltage commands on the bench and showed that a request stays on the motor after the release, which is why every hold got a stop.
videos.handsTo: Conditions and Logging starts from commands that hold a target and never end, and gives a routine a way to know the mechanism has arrived.
lines: On the bench last time, a request that stayed on the motor after you let go was the problem. Now your code sends the request you already ran in Tuner X, and staying becomes useful.
That Control drop-down was picking a control request the whole time. The class in Java carries the same name, so there's nothing new to learn here. One field gets swapped.
Here's the swap. The old field named a voltage. This one names a target angle, and the motor works out the smooth ramp that gets the arm there.
The commands change with it. The two that pushed volts become two that each name a place, and the stop stays, because you may still want out partway through a move.
Each command is a single line. It says where the arm should be, in rotations, and it never finishes, so it keeps asking for that spot for as long as it runs.
Down here is where the target reaches the motor. The number goes into the request, and the request goes out.
Then the binding. The trigger starts the new command, and the piece that stopped the arm on release comes out.
This is last lesson's surprise turned around. Canceling still sends the motor nothing, so the last request stays, only now it's a place to hold and not a push that never ends.
Run it on the bench and watch two things. The arm stops at vertical by itself however long you hold, and it's still there after you let go.
If nothing moves at all, the values in your config are probably still zero, so paste it in again. Overshooting and hunting is a tuning problem, and that gets fixed in Tuner X.
Both new commands name a target and never finish. Nothing in the code can tell yet when the arm has arrived, and a routine will need to know.

videos.title: Conditions and Logging
videos.opensFrom: Motion Magic in Code left the arm driving to an angle from a held trigger, on a command that never ends.
videos.handsTo: Coroutines writes routines whose waits are built on the arrival check, with the log already running.
lines: Your arm now drives to an angle on Motion Magic while you hold a trigger. That command never ends on its own, so nothing in your code can say when the arm got there.
Arriving needs a tolerance, and picking it is a judgment call. A real sensor never sits perfectly still, so waiting for an exact match means waiting forever.
Then three small methods. Two only report: where the arm is right now, and where it's headed, read straight off the request you're already sending.
The third compares those two using your tolerance. Every routine you write later asks this question, so how close counts gets decided in one place.
An answer you can't see is hard to trust, so record it. Two lines at the top of the robot's constructor start a log file that runs for as long as the program does.
The second of those lines is the one people skip. It adds the driver station's side: whether the robot was enabled and what the sticks were doing.
The arm writes its own signals. Each one gets a name here, and those names are what you'll look for when you open the file.
Notice there's no unit conversion anywhere. The value goes in with its unit attached, and you choose degrees or rotations later, on the graph.
None of that runs until the robot calls it. One line for each mechanism, every loop, in a method that runs in every mode, so the log keeps going when your command doesn't.
Run it in hardware sim and move the arm twice. Then disable before you stop the program, or the last few entries never reach the file.
Open the newest log in AdvantageScope before you start the program again, because a file that hasn't been renamed yet gets deleted on the next start.
This is the check. The position catches up to the target, and the arrival signal turns true when they meet. A routine can wait on exactly that, which is the next lesson.

videos.title: Coroutines
videos.opensFrom: Conditions and Logging gave the arm and the flywheel a logged answer to whether they have arrived; nothing waits on that answer yet.
videos.handsTo: The arm and flywheel now run a routine with no driver; Swerve Basics leaves the bench mechanisms and starts on the drivetrain.
lines: Your arm and flywheel can both say whether they've arrived, but nothing waits for that answer yet. A coroutine does. It's a routine that can stop on a line until something comes true.
Four calls build every routine in this course. Two of them start a command, and the other two only wait.
The arm's command never finishes on its own. Await it, and the routine never leaves that line, so anything that runs forever gets forked instead.
Don't drop the little arrow in front of the question. It's what lets the routine ask again on every loop, instead of asking once and keeping a stale answer.
Here's the first routine, on the Y button. Read it straight down: send the arm up, wait for it, send it down, wait again, print.
The flywheel's routine ends differently. Canceling a command doesn't stop a motor, so the routine sends the stop itself before it runs out of lines.
A routine is plain Java, so a loop just works. Same four lines, three times round.
Every routine on the page has a timeline behind its code. On this one, look at the arm's lane. It keeps moving while the routine is parked on a wait.
Autonomous changes one thing. Nobody's holding a button, so nobody can let go, and a wait that never comes true would sit there for the whole period.
So every wait gets a limit. Then check which ending you got, because a wait that ran out carries straight on as if the arm had arrived.
Once the flywheel is spinning, every way out stops it first. There are two here, the early one and the normal one.
Now look at the two lanes together. The arm's command is still running underneath while the flywheel spins up and the shot happens, which is the whole reason it was forked.
Before you move on, break it on purpose, twice, and see what each change does. That's the bench mechanisms done. Next the course moves to the drivetrain.

videos.title: Swerve Basics
videos.opensFrom: Coroutines left an arm and a flywheel running whole routines, from a button and in autonomous, on a robot that never moved.
videos.handsTo: Swerve Project Generator puts all thirteen devices on one bus, assigns them corner by corner, and has Tuner X write the constants file.
lines: So far you've been running one arm and one flywheel. Now the whole robot moves, and the next few lessons assume you know the words on this page.
The four corners are named from behind the robot. Stand in front of it instead and left and right swap, so pick your spot before you name anything.
A module is where the new trick happens. Two motors share one wheel, so it can roll and aim at the same time.
One gyro tells the robot which way it's facing. You'll need it again in a minute. The bus adapter is the same part from your bench.
Count them up and it's thirteen devices on one bus. You won't write the math that coordinates eight motors, though. That gets generated for you in the next lesson.
There are two ways to drive it. Robot-centric sounds simple until the robot turns to face you, and then pushing the stick away brings it straight at you.
Field-centric fixes that, because away from you always means away from you. It only works if the robot knows its heading, which is why the gyro is on the parts list.
The next three terms stack. A spot on the field, then a heading, then the two together, and that last one describes both where the robot is and where you want it to go.
Odometry is the robot's own running estimate of that pose, built from nothing but how far its wheels turned. A wheel that slips still counts, so the estimate drifts.
This is the frame those numbers live in. Everything is measured from the blue corner, with X running down the field and Y running across it to the left.
It doesn't flip when you're on red. A red robot sitting at its own wall reports a large X, so don't expect zero there.
Before you go on, stand behind a real robot with the power off and find all thirteen devices. The generator in the next lesson needs every one of them assigned to its corner.

videos.title: Swerve Project Generator
videos.opensFrom: Swerve Basics named the four corners, the thirteen devices on one bus, and field-centric driving, and sent the student to find every device on a real robot.
videos.handsTo: Swerve Drive Tuning takes the generated constants file, whose gains and measurements are still guesses, and tunes the steer motors, wheel radius, top speed and drive loop.
lines: You've found all thirteen devices on the robot. Now Tuner X measures the drivetrain and writes one file about it, so get the robot up on blocks first.
The generator would happily write a whole project. You don't need one. Yours is already written, and all it's missing is the numbers for your robot.
Start with the device list: thirteen devices on one bus, no two sharing an ID. Write them down by corner, because the wizard asks which ones sit where.
Then four numbers, off a tape measure and not the CAD. Both distances run between module centers.
Each corner gets its encoder and two motors, then a calibration with the wheel straight. If a different corner moves during the checks, its devices are assigned to the wrong module.

Slow down here. Generate only the constants, not a project, and put that file over the one already in yours. Then fix one import near the top, because the generator still writes the old folder name, and the build stops on that line until you do.
Keep a hand on disable. Enabled with nobody touching the controller, nothing should move. On the floor, turn the robot ninety degrees and push forward, and it should head the same way as before.
No robot yet? Plain simulation runs the same code with no hardware at all, and later swerve lessons lean on it.
Your own drivetrain commands go in the drivetrain class, and that's what your OpModes talk to. Tuner X only ever writes the constants file, so pasting in a new one never touches them.
Remember that a canceled command leaves its last request in the motors. For a drivetrain that's a speed, so the robot would keep rolling.
So the drivetrain gets a default command that reads the sticks every loop. Let go and it's still running, just asking for zero. It's set in the robot, not an OpMode, so every mode has it.
The left bumper makes wherever the robot faces now the new forward. The numbers in your new file are only a starting point, though, and tuning them comes next.

videos.title: Swerve Drive Tuning
videos.opensFrom: Swerve Project Generator left a robot that drives on a generated constants file, with the generator's own gains and measurements still in it.
videos.handsTo: Autonomous needs a robot you can drive with a pose you trust, and sends it off the starting line with nobody on the sticks.
lines: The generator handed you a robot that drives, on a file full of guesses. Now you replace them with measured numbers, starting with the motors that aim the wheels.
Steering is a position loop with nothing pulling it down, so the gravity gain drops out. You're adjusting the generator's numbers, not starting from zero.
Flick the stick and watch the measured angle chase the commanded one. If it lags, shoots past or buzzes, change one number, redeploy, and flick again.
Wheel radius is the one you can probably skip. Only measure it if you've changed wheels, or the robot's idea of distance disagrees with a tape measure.
Here the robot went less far than it reported, so the radius in the file was too big, and it comes down.
Top speed has a trap. Full stick asks for exactly the number in the file, so a plateau sitting right on it tells you nothing about the robot. Raise it until the robot falls short.
Slip current needs a wall and one drive motor, with the voltage ramped up slowly.
Watch for the instant velocity jumps and current drops. That's the tire letting go, and you want the peak just before it.
Keep each ramp short. A motor pushing a wall it can't move is stalled, and it heats up fast.
The drive gains only matter because every drive request in this course asks for a wheel speed. The generator's version sends the stick straight to volts and never reads them.
On a speed loop, feedforward does nearly all of the work, so it's tuned first. Keep the wheels on the ground, because a wheel in the air has no load.
The deadband keeps a worn stick from creeping the robot across the field. Halve it until the wheel targets twitch with your hands off, then go back one.
Drive a square, and check that the robot comes back to its tape with the pose near zero. Autonomous leans on that pose next, with nobody on the sticks.

videos.title: Autonomous
videos.opensFrom: Swerve Drive Tuning ended with the robot driven around a square by hand, back on its tape mark with a pose you can trust.
videos.handsTo: BLine Paths keeps this timed routine and adds a second one beside it that follows a path drawn in an editor.
lines: You finished tuning by driving a square back onto the tape. Now the robot drives with nobody on the sticks, in the same kind of class you wrote once already for the arm and flywheel.
Don't expect accuracy from this one. A timer is enough to prove the pieces talk to each other, and that's the only job it has today.
Forward here means the robot's own forward, not the field's. Whichever way the front bumper points on the tape mark is the way it leaves.
The command itself is three steps: start driving, wait, send a stop. A wait is the only finish line you've got, because nothing on the drivetrain can say it has arrived.
A cancel skips whatever was left, and that includes the stop. So the canceled branch sends the same zero, and the wheels never depend on hands staying off the sticks.
The class around it stays thin. One method schedules the routine on enable, and there's nothing to write for the end, because leaving the mode cancels the routine for you. A disable counts.
Run it in the simulator first and watch the pose. Stopping isn't enough. It has to stay stopped, because a request nobody replaces keeps the wheels turning.
Set the room up before you enable. One person watches the robot, one keeps a thumb near disable, and enabling comes last.
Then the floor, with clear space ahead. It leaves the way its front bumper points, so aim the robot before you enable, not after.
A second routine is just a second file, and it shows up on the list by itself. Next, the timer goes, and a drawn path tells the robot where to drive instead of how long.

videos.title: BLine Paths
videos.opensFrom: Autonomous left a Leave Start routine that drives on a timer, which proves the mode runs and says very little about where the robot ended up.
videos.handsTo: Every path here was drawn ahead of time; Drive to Point builds a one-waypoint path in code at the moment a button is held.
lines: Leave Start drove on a timer, and a timer can't tell you where the robot ended up. This time you draw where it should go, and a library does the driving.
Nothing to install this time. The library came with the swerve project, and the paths you draw live in one folder that ships to the robot with every deploy.
The path itself is short. A waypoint where the robot starts, one point to drive to, and a rotation that turns it along the way.
The event is the part to get exactly right. Its key is only a name, and your code looks up that same name later. One wrong capital and nothing runs.
Before you export, delete any path you made and left empty. It exports with the rest, and the robot throws an error when it loads it.
There's nothing to type on the robot side. The follower's already built into the drivetrain class, and its arguments teach the library this robot: where it is, how fast it's moving, how to drive it.
Three controllers pull the robot back onto the path. Their values were only tuned in simulation, so on a real robot they're a place to start.
Leave Start stays. The new autonomous class goes in beside it, and both show up on the driver station's list.
First the path becomes a command. The file's read right here, so a misspelled name fails the moment you pick the mode.
The pose reset on that line matters more than it looks. Leave it off, and the robot drives the right shape in the wrong place.
One class can hold several routines. A drop-down on the dashboard picks which, and one choice does nothing at all.
The choice is read at enable, not when the mode is picked, since somebody can still change the drop-down in between. Nothing here cancels the routine. Leaving the mode does that.
Last, give the event something to run. It's registered before any path gets built, and this one only prints a line.
In simulation the pose should jump to the start, and the event should print once per run. Every path so far was drawn ahead of time. Next, the robot builds one while you hold a button.

videos.title: Drive to Point
videos.opensFrom: BLine Paths replaced the Leave Start timer with a path drawn in the editor, exported, and followed as a command.
videos.handsTo: The robot only reaches the spot its pose points at; Vision Hardware mounts the camera that keeps that pose true.
lines: Last time you drew a path in the editor and the robot followed it. This path has a single stop, and nobody draws it. You hold a button, and the robot goes there.
The target is a spot on the field, measured from the blue corner. The robot only gets there if it knows where it's standing right now, and wheels alone lose track.
A drawn path is only a list that gets read from a file, so the same list can be built in code. Here it has one entry.
Look at what's missing. There's no starting point anywhere, because the path begins wherever the robot happens to be when the command starts.
It comes out of the same builder as your drawn paths, so it gets the same controllers, the same speed limits, and the same idea of close enough.
The alliance flip comes along too. You write the goal for blue, and on red the same button drives to the matching spot on your own side of the field.
Two buttons, two spots. One brings the robot back to the field origin, and the other sends it a few meters away, turned to face the opposite direction.
Both are held, not tapped. Let go partway and the command is canceled, with a zero sent on the way out, so the robot stops where it is.
Once it arrives, the command is over. Your sticks have the drivetrain back, even with the button still down.
When you test it, don't skip the third step. Run the far spot on blue, switch to red, and run it again. The second time it should finish at the other end of the field, facing the other way.
That's why you look at the alliance before holding the button on a real robot. On a floor with no field, red puts the target a whole field length away, and the robot will try to get there.
Any spot you can write as a coordinate, the robot can now drive to. It's only as good as the pose it starts from, and the camera that keeps that honest comes next.

videos.title: Vision Hardware
videos.opensFrom: Drive to Point sends the robot to a field pose, and it only arrives if the pose it believes is true.
videos.handsTo: A camera that reports a tag at the right distance, and its name; Vision feeds those sightings into the pose estimator.
lines: Drive to Point only works if the robot knows where it's standing. A camera is how it finds out, and none of this is code yet.
Wheels lose a little ground the longer you drive, and they never get it back. A tag sits at a known place on the field, so a sighting late in a match is as good as one at the start.
It isn't a replacement, though. Sightings come now and then, and they're noisy, so the robot keeps its odometry and blends the two.
We use a Limelight, with the camera and processor in one sealed unit. On PhotonVision, the ideas still carry over.
Pick the mounting spot by thinking about the moment you score. That's when the pose has to be right, so that's when the camera needs a tag in view.
Seen straight on from its own height, a tag is a plain rectangle, and a tiny error in one corner swings the answer a long way. From off to one side, the shape tells the camera far more.
On the Limelight 3 and 4, we've found the lens doesn't come glued, so you may want to glue yours.
Six steps, and the order matters. The field map comes first, because a camera still running last season's map puts every tag in the wrong spot.
Then the AprilTag pipeline, since a color pipeline never reports a position at all. Turn the exposure down as far as the camera can stand, so a moving robot doesn't blur the tag.
The camera only ever solves for where the camera is. The offsets move that answer to the middle of the robot, so if they're wrong, every reading is off the same way.
Calibration takes out the bend in the lens, which is worst near the edges of the picture. Then write down the camera's name, because that's how the code will find it.
Now test it. Hold a tag about a meter out and check the distance against a tape measure. Once they agree, the code can start feeding these sightings into the pose.

videos.title: Vision
videos.opensFrom: Vision Hardware left a camera mounted, calibrated and named, and a robot that still ignores what it sees.
videos.handsTo: The field pose now gets corrected by tags; Align to Tag skips the field pose and lines up on a spot measured from one tag.
lines: Your camera's mounted, calibrated and named, and the robot still ignores it. This is where the wheels stop being the only opinion about where the robot is.
Nothing to install. The camera library came with the swerve project, so all you write is one class that passes what the camera sees to the drivetrain.
The camera answers every frame twice. The first works out heading from the tags themselves, and with one tag in view, a tiny error in the corners throws it off.
The second takes your gyro's heading on faith and only solves for position. One tag is plenty, but a bad heading comes back as a wrong position that looks fine.
Every loop, the heading goes out to the cameras first, because that second answer depends on it. Then it reads a queue, since camera frames and robot loops don't tick together.
Each frame gets asked the first way. Fewer than two tags in that answer, and the same frame is asked again the second way.
Some sightings get thrown out. The library has its own checks, and anything averaging past four meters never reaches the estimator.
What's left goes in with the picture's own timestamp. The photo's already old when your code sees it, so the estimator winds back to that moment and folds it in there.
Every sighting also says how far off it might be, and distance makes that worse slowly. A second tag cuts it to a quarter, more than halving the distance would.
And when the second answer was used, its heading is ignored. That heading was yours to begin with, so it tells the estimator nothing new.
It all starts from one line in the robot class, not in an OpMode, because those get thrown away on every mode switch. The name in quotes has to match the camera's exactly.
Cover the camera, push the robot sideways, then uncover it. The pose should settle back. Next, the robot lines up on a single tag without asking where it is on the field.

videos.title: Align to Tag
videos.opensFrom: Vision fed AprilTag sightings into the pose estimator, behind trust gates, so the camera pulls the field pose back toward the truth.
videos.handsTo: This closes the main course; the optional Mechanism Simulation extra stands a physics model in for a mechanism that isn't built yet.
lines: Last lesson, the camera started correcting where the robot thinks it is on the field. Now it lines the robot up on one tag, and the field pose never comes into it.
A spot measured from a tag needs the tag's own axes. Straight out of its face is forward, and a robot looking squarely at the tag reads a half turn.
The camera reports the same thing with its axes pointed other ways, so this small method swaps them around. Every sign in it matters.
Get one backwards and the robot heads the wrong way at full speed, so the first check on this page happens before anything drives.
Here's the idea the lesson rests on. The camera is slow, and it loses the tag up close, so a sighting only has to put the tag down. The wheels carry the robot from there.
The new call runs ahead of the trust checks from last time. One close tag is exactly what those throw out, and it's the one sighting this needs.
Each sighting looks up where the robot was when the picture was taken, then places the tag from there. It also logs a number you'll read later.
The driving is the builder you already know from Drive to Point. What changed is where it gets its pose, which now comes from the tag.
Losing the tag on the way in doesn't stop it, because the wheels finish from the last sighting. And if no camera has ever seen that tag, the robot is told it's already there, so nothing moves.
Don't reach for a tape measure. Park the robot by hand where it should score, read the numbers the camera gives you, and type those in. Whatever's off about the camera's mount cancels out.
Then do it again at the event, before your first match. Tags are mounted by hand, so every field differs a little.

The third check is the one only this lesson has. Cover the camera, shove the robot sideways so its field pose is wrong, and it still stops on the same spot. That's the main course done, and mechanism simulation is an extra.

videos.title: Mechanism Simulation
videos.opensFrom: The main course is finished, and the arm and flywheel code from Coroutines has only ever run against real motors on the bench.
videos.handsTo: This is the last lesson; the gains found here fit a model, and they get tuned again on the mechanism once it is built.
lines: Everything you've written so far ran on a real motor on the bench. If your own robot isn't built yet, the same code can run against a physics model instead.
You've used Hardware Sim, where the laptop stood in for the robot controller. Here the motors are simulated too, and a simulated motor has nothing to turn.
The file to read is the sim class. It opens with the real arm written down as numbers, and the simulation is only as good as they are.
The physics comes from the library, an arm swinging on one joint under gravity. It asks for every number up front, which means there's no setting you can forget.
Every loop is three steps. The motor's voltage goes into the model, the model moves the arm forward one tick, and the result goes back into the simulated sensors for your code to read.
Two calls at the end of the constructor hook it in. The picture runs everywhere, because it only draws what the motor reports. The sim gets built only when there's no real arm.
Nothing gets added to the robot class. The sim only lasts as long as whatever built it, so a mechanism made inside an OpMode stops simulating when that OpMode ends.
Run it as it ships and nothing moves, because every gain starts at zero. Put in your own starting values first.
Once you're enabled, open the arm's picture. Hold a button, and a thin grey line shows where the closed loop is trying to take it.
Tune in the same order as in Tuner X, changing the number in code and restarting between tries. The result fits a model, not your mechanism.
For your own design, the motor changes in two places. The simulated Talon assumes a different one unless told, and left that way, the bench arm ran away from its target.
You're done when the orange line settles on the grey one. That's the end of the course, and the next arm you tune should be a real one.
